name: Weaving Fragments, Weaving Memory
description:
Group portrait featuring Rajah Gokuldas of Jubbulpore, Lawrie Art Studio, Jubbulpore, 1880s, Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh, Silver gelatin print, PHY.02467
Join us for a hands-on album-making workshop inspired by the muraqqa—a pre-modern album in which paintings, photographs, texts, and other fragments are assembled into a larger whole.
Led by Rohini Kejriwal, the workshop will explore image-text relationships, and the ways in which juxtaposition, annotation, and sequencing can weave together personal narratives. Participants will create a tangible artefact to take home, bringing together materials, memories, and stories of their own.
Participants are encouraged to bring old photographs, artworks, texts, or other ephemera they would like to incorporate into their personal muraqqa.

name: Reimagining the Muraqqa: Deaf-Led Walkthrough
description:
Join us for a deaf-led walkthrough of our latest exhibition, Reimagining the Muraqqa, with Akanksha Kamble from the Inclusions team, as she illuminates the artworks on display through Indian Sign Language (ISL).

The exhibition brings together traditional paintings from the personal collection of writer, photographer, and artist Waswo X. Waswo, generously gifted to MAP. Many of these paintings were inexpensive works sold as “antiquities” or what he came to call heritage paintings and, over time, these seemingly modest objects have revealed a complex visual record of a changing India.

Drawing on the muraqqa - a pre-modern album in which paintings, photographs, and other fragments are assembled into a larger whole, the exhibition considers how narratives, memories, and associations can emerge through juxtaposition, annotation, and the act of looking.

name: Three Women and a Camera
description:
Join us for a screening of a documentary by Sabeena Gadihoke on 3 female photographers: Homai Vyarawalla, Sheba Chhachhi and Dayanita Singh. 

Three Women and a Camera is a film about Homai Vyarawalla, India’s first woman photojournalist for three decades from the late 1930s, and two contemporary female photographers — Sheba Chhachhi and Dayanita Singh. Vyarawalla’s work underscores the optimism and euphoria of the birth of a nation, while Chhachhi and Singh attempt to grapple with the complexities and undelivered promises of the post-independence era. This film debates their concerns regarding representation, subject-camera relationships, and the limits and possibilities of still photography in India in the late 1990s.

The film Three Women and a Camera has won several awards, including the second prize at Film South Asia, a documentary festival in Kathmandu, Nepal, 1999 and a Certificate of Merit at the Mumbai International Film Festival for animation, documentary and short films, 2000.

This event is part of Art is Life: Elsewhere  hosted in collaboration with Bangalore International Centre, as an offshoot series of programs as part of our annual festival Art is Life.

name: Neural Naatak: A Techno-Magic Performance
description:
Neural Natak is a speculative fiction performance by Mumbai-based artist Spryk that imagines neural networks as practitioners of technomagic—an ancient-future craft where technology and illusion merge. The performance fuses cutting-edge Gen-AI visuals & electronic music, inspired by Indian street magic & ritual theatre, into a mixed-media performance, exploring how archival intelligence remembers these rarely documented yet rich subcultures from India’s past. The soundtrack for Neural Natak features electronic music production informed by more traditional musical structures, creating a grand soundstage. The score is interwoven with folk percussion-inspired layered rhythms accentuated with razor-sharp textures.

This event is part of Art is Life: Elsewhere  hosted in collaboration with Goethe Institut/Max Mueller Bhavan, as an offshoot series of programs as part of our annual festival Art is Life.

name: From Stone to Story: Odissi through Sculpture
description:
Explore the relationship between visual art and movement in this immersive Odissi workshop. Beginning with a sculpture, participants will discover how Odisha’s artistic traditions have shaped the classical dance form, exploring its vocabulary through body awareness, Chauka, Tribhangi, mudras, rhythm and abhinaya.

Through demonstrations, discussions and hands-on exercises, participants will experiment with translating visual forms into movement and storytelling. The session will culminate in a collaborative movement composition, followed by learning a simple Odissi phrase and reflecting on the artwork that inspired the experience.

This workshop is part of the ongoing series, Responding to Art through the Arts. Facilitated by arts practitioners, it aims to activate MAP’s galleries through a series of workshops that hold space for young people’s responses to artwork on display. 

It is conducted as part of our engagements for the MAP Youth Collective – a community for young people (18-25 year olds) to engage with the arts and culture sector. The collective is for, of and by young people — to explore our shared identities and interests through art

name: Book Talk - Absolute Jafar
description:
Join us for a conversation around comic artist Sarnath Banerjee’s book, Absolute Jafar. 

Set in a world where bureaucracies and borders shape human relationships, Sarnath Banerjee’s Absolute Jafar is a poignant meditation on belonging and becoming. Perhaps the author’s most personal work yet, it is a bittersweet rhapsody, rich in humanity, wit and imagination. Moderated by Arundhati Ghosh, the conversation reflects Sarnath’s practice, influences and the ideas behind the book.

In conjunction with the exhibition A Moving Line: 1500 Years of Indian Visual Storytelling.

name: From Miniature to Bazaar: Art, Patronage and Visual Culture
description:
Join us for a conversation on the visual worlds brought together in our latest exhibition, Reimagining the Muraqqa.

Dr Ranu Roychoudhuri and Rucha Vibhute will consider miniatures, silver gelatin photographs depicting late nineteenth-century royalty, and painted photographs—forms with distinct origins that converge in the embellished image to generate new narratives. The discussion will explore how artistic practices evolved across media, shaped by patronage and circulation, and how they found their way into popular visual culture through bazaar art.

Moving beyond questions of influence and origin, the conversation will attend to the subjects, stories, and ways of seeing that emerge when these images are read alongside one another.

name: Reimagining the Muraqqa: Designer POV
description:
A Shaivite Pandit, Not yet identified artist, Late 19th to early 20th century, Rajasthan, Pigment painting on paper, PTG.02502

Join us for a walkthrough of MAP’s latest exhibition, Reimagining the Muraqqa, with designer Rishabh Jain and co-curator Vineet Kajrolkar.

Drawing on the muraqqa—a pre-modern album in which paintings, photographs, and other fragments are assembled into a larger whole—the exhibition considers how narratives, memories, and associations emerge through juxtaposition, annotation, and the act of looking. In this walkthrough, Jain and Kajorlkar will reflect on the design decisions, spatial choices, and curatorial ideas that shape visitors’ encounter with the works.

name: Reimagining the Muraqqa: Curator POV
description:
Join our curators, Rucha Vibhute and Vineet Kajrolkar, for a walkthrough of our latest exhibition, Reimagining the Muraqqa—which brings together traditional paintings from the personal collection of writer, photographer, and artist Waswo X. Waswo, generously gifted to MAP. 

Many of these paintings were inexpensive works sold as “antiquities” or what he came to call heritage paintings and, over time, these seemingly modest objects have revealed a complex visual record of a changing India.

Drawing on the muraqqa - a pre-modern album in which paintings, photographs, and other fragments are assembled into a larger whole, the exhibition considers how narratives, memories, and associations can emerge through juxtaposition, annotation, and the act of looking.

name: A Moving Line: 1500 Years of Indian Visual Storytelling - Curator Walk-through
description: Join us for a guided walkthrough of the A Moving Line: 1500 Years of Indian Visual Storytelling as Khushi Bansal from MAP narrates the stories this country tells through lines. In this exhibition, one can witness both the creation of new visual identities and the evolution of a nation through a vast body of works across time and space. Here, kaavad and pattachitra scroll sitting alongside Amar Chitra Katha and Tinkle. Chacha Chaudhary next to the Phantom, while contemporary graphic novels and web comics continue conversations that began centuries ago.

name: In the Company of Trees
description:
Under the canopy of the trees in your neighbourhood, many stories unfold, but who are these trees–what are their names and their puzzles and wonders? 

Join us for a workshop that brings together a guided nature walk of the Mahalaxmi Layout neighbourhood in Bengaluru by Kavya Chandra and a cyanotype and overdyeing workshop by Gunjan Pramod. You’ll be introduced to the different trees that make up this locale, pick up leaves, odd seedpods and other organic material to make your own prints using the cyanotype method. During the printmaking session, you will also be introduced to overdyeing processes using natural pigments.

name: Learning Contexts: Archives in Educational Settings
description:
Many contemporary archival practices treat their work as material that engages public memory in the present; they’re not simply driven towards finding, guarding and building safe repositories. They consider what archives can offer in challenging established narratives and providing a framework for engaging with underrepresented histories. How can these ideas be tinkered around with in educational settings, and what can that offer to pedagogy? Through this discussion, we will engage with archives that operate out of, or work with, educational institutions in different registers to understand how their practices enter learning contexts and what the future of their work looks like.

We will be joined by Anjali Ramachandran from the Archives at the National Centre for Biological Sciences (NCBS) and Mira Brunner from the Queer Archive for Memory, Reflection, and Activism (QAMRA) at National Law School of India University (NLSIU) in conversation with Dr Samyak Ghosh, Assistant Professor, Social Science at NLSIU.

This event is part of Art is Life: Elsewhere hosted in collaboration with National Law School of India University (NLSIU), as an offshoot series of programs as part of our annual festival Art is Life.

name: A Closer Look | Ayodhya: Epicentre of a Divide
description:
Join photo-journalist, Prashant Panjiar and writer Valay Singh for a moderated conversation on the launch of the latest photo book, 'Ayodhya: Epicentre of a Divide'.

The book covers nearly four decades of Ayodhya: its ghats and akharas, Sufi shrines and Hanuman temples, barricades and barbed wire, and the laser shows and hoardings of the new temple town. With an essay by Valay Singh on how Ram was turned into a political symbol, this book is a rare long view of a fabled town that became the epicentre of a campaign to reshape India.

name: A Closer Look: The Painted Imaginaries of Fiza Khatri
description:
Brick Library, 2026, 59 x 85 inches, oil on canvas. Courtesy the artist and Jhaveri Contemporary.
In The Great Rebuild!, artist Fiza Khatri's recent body of work, they invite us into the playful world of children. We see them inhabiting the shifting terrain between play and reality, transforming everyday objects into vessels for imagined journeys. Their irreverent world-building mimics the war and destruction they see around them, building shelters from sofa cushions, playing doctor-patient. Here, building and unbuilding become gestures of possibility, and play becomes a way of rehearsing, reflecting upon and remaking the conditions of existence.

In this edition of A Closer Look, Khatri takes us through the making of this series, and, more broadly, the evolving concerns that animate their practice at large. Across their practice, painting is as much an observational exercise as it is an exercise in imagination. Their paintings bring human and non-human figures into intimate, often unpredictable relationships, allowing bodies, objects, plants and landscapes to coexist without settling into fixed hierarchies or identities. Boundaries between the animate and inanimate, the familiar and the fantastical, tenderness and violence, the sacred and the everyday begin to dissolve. Their paintings invite a kind of looking that is also a form of sensing, or feeling, drawing from the material tactility of the medium itself: the weight, softness, texture or unruliness of things. Meaning is not always immediately legible; it takes shape through the layers that make their work, the stories they contain and the beauty they offer that is so deeply tied to the complexities of lived experience. Moving backwards through their practice, this talk considers how Khatri’s paintings create spaces in which different forms of life, knowledge and feeling might meet, and how painting can become a means of imagining ways of being together otherwise.

This programme at MAP is part of A Closer Look, a monthly series of research-focused talks by artists, curators and art historians focusing on visual cultures of South Asia

name: Reimagining the Muraqqa: Collector & Artist POV
description:
A Dream of Abundance, 2026, Waswo X. Waswo and Chirag Kumawat
Join us for a walkthrough of our latest exhibition, Reimagining the Muraqqa led by collector and artist, Waswo X. Waswo and Chirag Kumawat. Drawing on his personal collection, generously gifted to MAP, Waswo will share the journeys, encounters, and decisions that brought these works together.

From paintings acquired as “antiquities” to works that have come to reveal layered histories of making, collecting, and looking, this walkthrough offers a rare opportunity to hear the collector’s and artist's perspectives on the exhibition and the ideas and artistic traditions that inform it.

name: Reading the Muraqqa: Researcher POV
description:
Tantric card depicting Hayagriva Murti, Not yet identified artist, Late 20th century, Rajasthan, India, Pigment painting on paper, PTG.02506
Join researcher Yanush Batra for a walkthrough of Reimagining the Muraqqa, MAP’s latest exhibition.

The exhibition brings together traditional paintings from the personal collection of writer, photographer, and artist Waswo X. Waswo, generously gifted to MAP. Many of these works were originally inexpensive objects sold as “antiquities,” or what Waswo came to call heritage paintings. Over time, however, these seemingly modest works have revealed themselves to be a layered and complex visual record of a changing India.

Taking its title from the muraqqa—a pre-modern album in which paintings, photographs, calligraphy, and other fragments are assembled to form a larger whole—the exhibition explores how meaning can be created through juxtaposition, annotation, and sustained looking.

Rather than presenting these works as isolated objects, the exhibition invites viewers to consider the narratives, memories, and associations that emerge when images are placed in conversation with one another. Through this walkthrough, we'll trace the ideas and curatorial choices behind the exhibition, offering insights into the collection, the history and form of the muraqqa, and the ways in which these paintings invite us to rethink inherited categories of art.

name: Layers of Tradition: An Introduction to Miniature Painting
description: Join us for a close-looking session on select artworks from our latest exhibition, Reimagining the Muraqqa, with co-curator Vineet Kajrolkar. This will follow a hands-on session introducing materials, techniques, and the iconography of traditional Rajasthani miniature painting school with the artist Chirag Kumawat.

name: A Moving Line: 1500 Years of Indian Visual Storytelling - Designer’s Walkthrough
description:
Visual storytelling has always been a medium of documentation, communication and expression. While comics give voice to the voiceless, and articulates the ridicule we feel vis-à-vis the errors of power structures, it is also important to observe that a few bodies fall through the cracks of representation. Who decides who gets omitted? Who decides that every medium should follow standards set by the mainstream? Who defines these standards of what represents good or evil? And why shouldn’t comics question and redefine these standards?

Join us for a walkthrough by Neelima Aryan from the Design Team at MAP for a final walkthrough of the exhibition A Moving Line: 1500 Years of Indian Visual Storytelling.

name: Returning to the Family Album
description:
This 2-hour workshop invites participants to gather and write about or alongside family photographs–a small selection of images or subarchive of your choice from family albums that you wish to spend time with.

Through readings, guided prompts, and collective writing time, we’ll explore different ways of entering a photograph–through memory and nostalgia, absence and grief, grammar and aesthetic, personal and collective histories, fiction and speculation, research and restoration, political and social contexts, or simply as a way of staying related to someone within the photograph.

The session begins with a short lecture and discussion, followed by a focused 45-minute writing period, and concludes with some reflective time together. Participants are free to write in any form–poetry, letters, essays, notes, as research, or to inspire making a new artwork. This workshop emphasizes process over product; nothing will be shared or critiqued. This workshop is an invitation to return, unceremoniously but persistently, to look again and pay attention to a few photographs that ritualize remembering and writing, amidst so many others that constantly demand our time. This workshop is open to anyone and everyone. 

As part of Art is Life: Elsewhere this workshop is hosted as an offshoot series of programs hosted at partner venues across Bengaluru as part of our annual festival Art is Life.
